newsitem.title: USA: US governors ask Congress to keep ethanol subsidy.
newsitem.headline: US governors ask Congress to keep ethanol subsidy.

text.p: U.S. Midwest governors urged congressional leaders Monday to renew an ethanol subsidy that some Washington lawmakers are seeking to scrap.

In a letter addressed to House Speaker Newt Gingrich and House Minority Leader Richard Gephart, the Midwestern Governors' Conference said the Ethanol Fuel Tax Credit represented a positive boost for the U.S. economy.
Six governors attached their names to the letter Monday, and Iowa Gov. Terry Branstad said at a news conference that he expected all 12 Midwest governors would eventually sign.

"The Ethanol Fuel Tax Credit Incentive has provided tremendous benefits by generating domestic economic activity, reducing the budget deficit through expanding agricultural markets, reducing our trade imbalance, reducing imports for foreign oil and reducing air pollution," the letter said.

The governors' request came hours after Rep. Bill Archer, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, unveiled a tax cut proposal that would first reduce the subsidy and then eliminate it in the year 2000.
Branstad, speaking reporters at the conclusion of the two-day annual meeting of the Midwestern Governors' Conference, said Archer's proposal was "bad policy."
"Archer doesn't talk about the subsidies the oil industry gets," Branstad said.
Branstad said he thought the subsidy would be maintained by a "close vote" in the House Ways and Means Committee.
The Midwestern Governors' Conference is made up of the governors of Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota and Wisconsin.
